content.text: I upheld the key on all nine questions. Every challenged option rests on a reading the poem shuts out, and the reason can be pointed to in the text.

verdicts.reasoning: In line 22, 'thanked him for the answer' is a deliberate courtesy, so he does not ask out of unnoticed habit. Lines 33-34 show his hope was still active, since he slid toward the west road in the afternoons. That rules out option 2.
'Lied' sits inside 'I wanted a grandfather who... lied about the war.' It names a performance the boy would have preferred, not a suspicion about his own grandfather. Option 0 misreads the grammar.
'To make room for' and the bench being trucked 'to the depot' show displacement, not honor. The glass and the 'timetable under glass' set a scheduled modern order against his open-ended vigil.
The sequence 'at Easter, / then at Christmas, then I meant to write' traces neglect growing step by step. That undercuts any reading of pride.
The west arm faces 'the city road', the road the speaker took, and lines 33-34 end with 'to me.' The text ties the afternoon move to the speaker, not to the sun.
The simile comes inside 'I was ashamed... I wanted', so it is the fourteen-year-old's judgment. The later stanzas undercut it. Nothing in the poem gives the grandfather's own view of his life.
'I let you think the road was slow' admits guilt. It confesses that the speaker was the late arrival and offers the grandfather no reassurance.
Only option 3 links the worn west arm to the western bus the speaker took. The other options misread the details or overreach.

The allusion stresses humble, faithful waiting. In the poem nobody comes back while he is alive: Pavel never returns, and the speaker comes only after his death. The poem gives no support for a triumphant homecoming.

'I had my reasons' presents the silence as chosen. Line 16 ('I would not have had him looking back') and the closing 'I keep it shut... I do not sing' confirm it. Option 1's claim of helpless grief contradicts this.

The stillness in lines 10-12 comes at the point where the tune halts. The movement in line 21 carries the finished tune down the towpath. The poem never marks a shift into night, so option 1 has no textual support.
The terse sentences follow each attempt one at a time. The next ending 'holds' (line 19), which rules out a conviction that the boy will never finish the song.
The water is 'waiting, as it waited / for every boat you ever let go down.' The image is one of expectation, not mourning, so option 0's grieving nature is unsupported.
The speaker never contradicts herself. 'It was never for the want of notes' explains why the tune stopped. The final stanza shows she holds the ending, so option 3 fits.
She does not teach the boy the ending ('I keep it shut... I do not sing'), so option 1 misreads the poem. The keyed thesis matches the closing lock-gate image.
'As you did' signals close imitation of his father. Nothing suggests he is performing for his mother, and the speaker deliberately does not call to him.
'I have it still' directly refutes the claim that she has forgotten the ending. Lines 25-26 state the keyed reading outright.
The drivers take the tune 'down the towpath with them,' carrying it along as they haul their boats. Their quick adoption of it ('They will call it his by Sunday') undercuts any sense of reluctance.
'As far as you' and 'He stops there too' tie the halt to Tom's own stopping point, not to the boy's skill giving out.
'Lock-beam' gives the working setting and 'after tea' gives the time of day. The drying-yard belongs to the remembered past and gives no time.
'Waiting' and 'holds one foot' create suspense. No detail signals menace or danger to the boy.
She addresses 'Tom' directly and refers to the boy in the third person, so she is speaking to her dead husband, not her son.

Teodor is mourned in one stanza, but the poem as a whole moves from 'They tell me minus eighteen is a kindness' to 'a prayer / that should not be answered.' The challenged option's claim that the note and envelope are 'the only traces' of his life has no support in the text.

The stem asks how the note relates to the final stanza. 'Good in poor ground' points ahead to 'the long drought' and 'the world above gone wrong.' Nothing in the poem says dryness is a bigger danger than the cold.
The seed has eaten nothing and broken no rule, so the punishment reading fails. 'At least they let her up for spring' sets her case against the seed's, which has no promised return.
'They tell me' signals skepticism, but the tone is wry. Nothing in the poem rises to 'bitter fury.'
'I want it so badly I almost crack' shows strain that is still unresolved, not peace. 'Crack' carries both meanings, which ties back to 'splitting.'
The schoolroom is a simile, not a past use of the building. Dagny 'goes out humming,' which rules out fear. The details show rare, brief, routine visits followed by dark.

Nothing in the poem ties Dagny to the future, and the seed never chooses to look ahead instead of back. The contrast is impersonal routine against intimate care ('licked the flap,' 'salt and pipe smoke').
The speaker calls itself 'a speckled bean,' is still in storage, and speaks to Teodor at the end. No distractor fits the text.
The mountain 'has never wanted / anything,' so it cannot share the seed's hope of being planted. The poem sets the mountain's lack of desire against the seed's wanting.
'Forgive me, Teodor' comes right after 'a prayer / that should not be answered.' The guilt is about wishing for disaster, not about causing his death.
Each distractor contradicts the text: the poem is full of feeling, reports no current events, and never enters Dagny's thoughts.

The stanza ends in craving and self-judgment ('Forgive me,' 'I almost crack'), not calm acceptance. It moves from purpose ('made for one thing, which is splitting') to cost (fire, war, drought) to judging itself.
The coin simile ('to be worth something, never spent') separates having value from being used. The distractors have no basis in the text.
The skeptical frame ('They tell me... a kindness') undercuts any reading of pride. The nested enclosures and cold suggest burial, which points ahead to the underworld allusion.

content.text: I upheld the key on all 13 items. Each challenged option fails for a specific reason in the text, and none of the challenges is a reasonable second answer.

verdicts.reasoning: The stem asks about the passage as a whole. The kitchen scene shows that Harrowby's exact manner covers a deliberate kindness that leaves Venn's pride alone. 'Cares more for rules' fits only a reading that stops before that scene.
'I was then seventeen' and 'I have since learned' show the story is told long after the events, by an older narrator looking back. That rules out a diary written as events happen.
The boats are 'cattle that had given up', the coble is a 'black scab' and the net is empty. All of this reflects Venn's stranded, worn-out working life. Nothing supports the other options.
Turning the cap 'as a man turns a coin he suspects' signals distrust of the offer. Venn never asks for more money and turns the offer down outright, so the bargaining reading fails.
'Figures... kept only by being left out' refers to Harrowby's private kindness, not falsified Trust books. The narrator learns that some kindness survives only if it goes unrecorded.

The reader shares the young clerk's misjudgment of Harrowby until the reveal. The other options misdescribe the narration: it never enters Venn's mind, does not give every motive equally and is not detached.

The question asks why the scene is withheld. The scene's placement mainly reverses our view of Harrowby and of Venn's refusal. 'Chronological shape' describes the order of events but gives no purpose, and the word 'strictly' overstates even that.

The housekeeper says the offer is made 'so that Venn may have the pleasure of refusing it', which directly supports the key. Nothing in the text shows that Venn knows who buys his fish or is grateful.
'Cattle that had given up' conveys tired resignation in things once made for work. None of the other options fits the image.
The older narrator's 'I am afraid with some heat' and his later change of view make the line about his proud handwriting read as self-mockery. A plain note on his penmanship ignores that context.
The fish are carefully weighed, yet the price paid is four times their quay value. So the exact weighing becomes a cover for generosity, not a symbol of the Trust's rigid fairness.
Of the four quotations, only the stack of unsigned earlier offers points to an offer that is repeated and refused each time. The others show only Harrowby's manner or Venn's unease.
The housekeeper quotes her master's own words, so nothing suggests she misunderstands his orders. The contrast shows that his cold talk of 'arithmetic' hid a deliberate tenderness.

Line 36 shows close noticing, like the same brown shoes 'resoled once in January.' That kind of attention goes against his claim that 'Wondering is for people on the bank.' Nothing in the text suggests he suspects fare-dodging, and she 'paid again.'
The reason he gives is circular and flat, which lets him avoid saying why she keeps riding. Nothing in the passage mentions money trouble, so option 0 adds facts the text doesn't support.
The fixed cable course sets up the needle metaphor and the ending, both about a confined, repeated path. The passage never says he admires machines.
'By the fourth crossing' the light has gone 'the color of weak tea,' which marks the afternoon fading over repeated trips. The other options have no basis in the text.
The thermos detail shows him changing what he does and then explaining it away, which is evidence of attention. 'It did not trouble me' is itself a claim of indifference, not proof of attention.
'A man could do worse' is a modest self-justification that hints at how narrow his life is. Option 3's 'superior to every other trade' claims much more than the text says.
Her own words support the key directly: 'I wanted to see if it got easier... It doesn't.' The other options depend on things the passage never says.

He adds a justification he didn't need ('There was no call to') right after he puts the thermos back and wipes the rail. That extra denial gives away the feeling. 'Fully accepted' and 'returned to contentment' go beyond the text.
We learn about her only through what he observes and reports. She is named in line 10, and we never get her inner thoughts, so options 2 and 3 are false.
He moved the thermos to the bench during her rides, and now he puts it back 'where it belongs.' That is restoring the old order. The other options are unsupported.
He has run the ferry 'since the spring of 1931' and tells the story in the past tense about October through March. The other options contradict the text.
The text says the hem 'never gets finished' and repeats 'It goes in and comes out,' so the image is endless repetition. That rules out a 'finished town.'

Telling us earlier that he lied about the count sets up dramatic irony for 'I didn't say.' Option 3 overstates a single detail ('values accurate records above all') and ignores why the placement matters.

The ending ('took them where they were going') shows that other people have destinations while he just shuttles back and forth. Mrs. Lorne leaves with a suitcase for the bus, so she has one too. Option 0 is contradicted by 'I did not watch the Cutbank side' and by his return to routine.

content.text:
The keyed answer is the best choice on all 14 items, and none of the challenged options is equally defensible.

One small wording issue in Question 3: the stem says line 6 comes "directly after" line 3, but lines 4–5 come between them. This is worth fixing, but it doesn't change which answer is correct.

verdicts.reasoning: 'your flask and your map' and 'tonight I'll tell you' show the father is absent. The walk is a report meant for him, not something he witnesses beside her.
'or weather' puts a plainer explanation next to the tender one, which undercuts confidence in strangers' devotion instead of supporting it.

Keys fasten the rails, so if the rails were scrapped, the keys went too. Coming right after the instruction to check them, the line shows the errand is odd. It is not a neutral fact. (Minor: lines 4–5 come between lines 3 and 6, so 'directly after' is loose.)
The stanza recasts the lie as a key 'driven / hard into the gap' to keep things steady. None of the other options fits.
'chair at Fairholme, brakes on' points to a wheelchair in a care home, and 'a ganger's' pace points to a track worker. 'tonight I'll tell you' shows he is alive.
'you knew' rules out confusion. The keys become the small fictions that keep father and daughter steady.
'you knew' rules out dementia, and 'the kind of lie you taught me' supports a shared, unspoken fiction, not pity.
'goes off like a dropped spanner' stresses a sudden, harsh noise and links it to a tool of track labor. It does not suggest delicacy.
The shoulder-high cow parsley and the dog walker's routine nod make the place overgrown and ordinary. The other options have no support.
'not the map. It's the walk' directly contradicts the idea that he has forgotten the route. His loss is bodily.
The empty cutting exposes the gap that leads to the insight 'you knew'. Line 23 at once overturns the 'out of date' reading.
The pun ties the dozing father to the track's last remaining part. 'still on the line' and 'tonight I'll tell you' show he is alive, so the elegy reading fails.
In the poem the wedge holds the heavy thing steady. The challenged option says it drives people apart, which reverses the image.

'you knew' shows his memory is intact, and 'I finish it for you, at your pace' shows her lending him her body. The challenged pair contrasts their bodies but contains neither the insight nor his intact memory.

content.text: I upheld the key on all 14 items. Each challenged option either contradicts the text or reads in something the poem doesn't contain.

verdicts.reasoning: The floor kept clean under the rugs looks ahead to what the house hid beneath its respectable surfaces, which stanzas 3-4 then reveal. Nothing in the text says the speaker wants the buyers to value the father's work, so [2] reads in a wish the poem never states.
'Raised better' ironically echoes a childhood spent learning to cover things up, which the poem exposes. Option [3] takes the line at face value as pride and ignores the irony the poem has built.
'Answers every foot' makes the house audible, and 'will not die' makes the furnace outlast its owners. Option [3]'s fear of a coming breakdown gets the furnace backwards.
'Everyone said so' marks the praise as the town's, and it turns ironic in stanza 4. Option [1] contradicts 'no neighbor ever heard'.
'I was eleven' is in the past tense, and the speaker drives away in a car. She is an adult, not a child.

The speaker takes back the accusation in line 20, and the poem never condemns the neighbors. Option [2] fails on both counts, while the key follows the poem's actual turn from accusing the house to confessing.

Stanza 4 is all sound: a chair against the door, a voice going small, a radio turned up. The violence is never shown directly. The house never speaks; the speaker is telling it, so [3]'s 'house's point of view' misreads the address to the house.
A jar holds things without will or judgment. Option [2] gives the house an intention ('chose to hide'), which the simile does not support.
'Going small' describes the mother's voice, not the music. The radio is being turned up, not fading out.
Option [0] claims nothing wrong happened, which contradicts stanza 4. The key captures the complexity: she disowns an accusation she has already largely made.
The 'bishop' simile and the theme of upbringing prepare for the Lot's wife allusion, so it is not a new note. The final line recasts her composed exit as a learned evasion, like turning up the radio.
Line 17 says the speaker, not the father, turned the radio up, so [2] has no textual basis.
'They'll mean it as a compliment' signals irony: the quiet the buyers praise is the same quality that once hid the trouble. Option [2] misses that irony.
The poem never makes claims about other houses in town, so [3] overreaches. The key traces the move from describing the house to confessing in line 17.

content.text:
All 13 keyed answers hold up, and none of the challenges shows a second defensible answer.

1. **Q1 – key holds.** The marks cannot be a fare calendar. She already owns the ticket, its "date gone by," and she says she counts "not for the ones who leave." The counting stands in for the trip she never takes.
2. **Q2 – key holds.** "She means it kindly" and the jug of water show warmth, not distance. Rent is never mentioned.
3. **Q3 – key holds.** "Now I am thorough" comes straight after "That one I did not count. / I did not know I was to keep the books." That makes the tone rueful. Pride in an earned escape is ruled out by "Not one of them has taken me."
4. **Q4 – key holds.** "Some parlor I will never sit in" stresses a place she is shut out of. Nothing in the poem shows envy of the owners.
5. **Q5 – key holds.** The memory of the uncounted six-ten makes the counting look like a response to that missed departure. Every distractor is contradicted by the text.
6. **Q6 – key holds.** A drawer opened in the dark and shut again is a brief, homely glimpse that is then withdrawn. No distractor has support in the poem.
7. **Q7 – key holds.** "Not for the ones who leave, but to be sure" states the claim directly. "Mrs. Pruett thinks I mean to go" only supports it by implication.
8. **Q8 – key holds.** "Complaint" gives the train's sound a note of grievance. The distractors (neighbors, open anger, old engines) have no textual basis.
9. **Q9 – key holds.** The short line "that I am here" sets apart the one fact the counting confirms. She neither resolves to leave nor stops counting.
10. **Q10 – key holds.** "Keep the books" is plainly an accounting metaphor. The added idea of "debt" goes a little beyond the text, but it is still clearly the best option.
11. **Q11 – key holds.** A first-person speaker cannot reveal the landlady's private thoughts. "Thinks I mean to go" is the speaker's own reading of her.
12. **Q12 – key holds.** "Wear that window thin" is Mrs. Pruett's figurative joke about the speaker's watching, not a physical feature of the room. The coal merchant's, the faded roses and the jug are the concrete details of a modest lodging.
13. **Q13 – key holds.** 411 tallies and an expired ticket point to a long stay, not a traveler briefly stranded.

verdicts.reasoning: Ticket already owned and expired; counting is 'not for the ones who leave'. Calendar-toward-fare reading unsupported.
'She means it kindly' and the water she brings signal tactful warmth; rent never mentioned.
'Now I am thorough' follows the uncounted departure of her brother; rueful fits. 'Not one of them has taken me' rules out pride in escape.
'Some parlor I will never sit in' stresses exclusion from destinations, not envy of wealth.
The memory recasts the counting as a response to the six-ten she 'did not count'; distractors contradicted.
Drawer opened and shut in the dark gives a brief, homely glimpse that is withdrawn; distractors unsupported.
'Not for the ones who leave, but to be sure' states the claim directly; the Pruett line is only indirect.
'Complaint' personifies the sound as grievance; distractors lack textual basis.
'that I am here' isolates her presence, the fact the counting confirms; other options contradict the poem.
'Keep the books' is an accounting metaphor, which ties it to the leaving she failed to mark.
A first-person speaker cannot reveal another's private thoughts; the reader sees that Pruett misreads her.
'Wear that window thin' is a figurative remark, not a physical detail of the room; the coal merchant's, faded roses and jug are concrete.
411 tallies and an expired ticket indicate a long-term lodger, not a briefly stranded traveler.

Option 3 claims that every memory is unreliable and that no past event can be known. Those absolute claims go far beyond the narrator's single dispute with one ledger entry. The key accounts for the ledger, the narrator's guarded insistence that she is practical, and the indirect admission at the end ('I find that I know all of them').

One remark about what dealers pay does not show 'thorough, expert' knowledge, and that reading misses why she says it. Just before it she says 'I did not wipe it.' She offers a commercial reason for not touching her father's things, which is what the key says.

The text never compares Pell's skill to the father's and never suggests Pell is dishonest. She never winds the clocks, so she is not eager to have them running. The loud watch in the silent room, and the line 'his watch went with him, and the shop was quiet again,' set ordinary commercial time against the shop's stopped time.

The simile describes someone waiting outside a sickroom, not the sick man's own fear, so option 2 assigns the feeling to the wrong person. 'Vigil' matches the waiting, held-breath image, and the earlier 'row of deacons' simile supports reading the whole shop as keeping watch. The stem is garbled ('that (lines 12-13)'), but that does not create a second defensible answer.

Nothing in the text builds suspense about Pell's offer, so option 3 only restates the order of events without naming an effect. Lines like 'when he looked at all' and 'It was always a clock that was nearly going' set up a feeling of neglect that the ledger later overturns.

Option 3 says both of them enjoyed a shared game, and the text gives no support for that. Her tone sounds like grievance. 'Though I had said nothing' shows he spoke to her without prompting, so he was aware of her, while she took his words as dismissal. That is the key.

Each distractor misdescribes this narration. She is not neutral, she has no access to her father's thoughts, and the point of view never shifts. Because we see the father only as she did, the ledger surprises both her and the reader.

Pell has just raised his offer, yet she sends him away ('You'll forgive me the trouble'), keeps the cash book and leaves the clocks unwound, so she is not haggling. Her refusal follows directly from finding the ledger, and she gives practical-sounding reasons instead of naming the feeling. That fits the key.

Lines 30-31 state a price, a month and a fact ('It's May. I'm full'). They refuse in flat business terms. Nothing defends the hotel's summer trade, and nothing suggests he thinks her rooms are cheap: he is offering more than a fair price.
Line 56 ('I was in pumps. For a while.') is what confirms the doubt about line 23. Option 1 says 'Pumps' proves he never sold a pump, and line 56 directly contradicts that.

She opens the key drawer, closes it without taking a key, then offers the kitchen room. That shows hesitation over a concession. Option 3's 'exact price she wants' has no support, because she names twelve only afterward and the gesture signals nothing to him.

'Walt' shows she recognized him, and 'eighteen years at nothing a year' turns the price into a debt. Option 1 is wrong because Walt already knows the bride is his daughter ('I only want to see her walk in').

Laying the key on the money keeps the exchange a sale and avoids touching him, which fits the claim. Option 1's 'only motive... profit' fails because she pockets the money with the hem pins, not in the till.
The heading changes only when Vera says 'Walt,' so the audience learns his name at the moment she reveals she knows it. Nothing in the text says the audience knew earlier, so option 0 has no basis.

Her precise memory of how he shut the door shows she still knows his small habits. The words 'always did' and 'decent enough' carry some reluctance. Nothing supports option 1's claims that she rehearsed the meeting or waited eighteen years.

She turns the photo face down, then looks at it, then turns it down again, which shows a divided impulse. Option 3's 'steady refusal... anything at all' is wrong because she tells him openly about the daughter's room, dress and wedding.

Asking 'And if I miss the bus?' hints that he wants to stay longer than the glimpse he claimed to want. Option 0 reverses this: missing the bus would keep him in town, not get him out before the ceremony.

She begins with 'We're full' to a stranger and ends with 'The house is asleep,' which echoes his own habit from lines 51-53, while still sending him up the back stairs. Option 2's 'exactly as guarded' and 'only' ignore that echo.

content.text: I upheld the key on all 14 items. None of the challenged options holds up against the text.

verdicts.reasoning: 'He made sure of that' blames her father for the language gap between them. Option 0 says he wrote the letter so she could never understand it, but he asked for it to be read to her, so the scene contradicts it.
Giving the original sentence first lets the reader catch the substitution as soon as it is spoken. Aurelio's 'That is not what I wrote' rules out any revision by him, so option 3 fails.

Her zipped coat and her standing instead of sitting show she is not settling in, and she sits only later. Nothing in the text says the room is badly heated, so option 3 adds a claim the passage does not make.
'I have held to it' states fidelity outright, and the flat list of very different cases shows professional evenness. Nothing in the text signals doubt about her accuracy.
'The agency called me' marks her as a hired professional, and 'who will drive in snow' is a dry joke about her usefulness. She is not a volunteer, so option 0 fails.
The fragments are her inner thoughts as she weighs the rule against the change she is about to make. They are not spoken aloud to Dana.
'Eu sei' is a private admission made in Portuguese, which Dana does not speak. It is neither open nor an apology.
The frozen trawlers and the image of plates left overnight in a sink set up a stalled scene left unattended. No other option has support in the text.
'Asked to work past its hours' makes the machine a tired worker, which points to his long, effortful dying. Nothing suggests a malfunction or neglect by staff.
Option 1 is only plot summary, and options 2 and 3 are unsupported or absolute claims. The key is specific and fits the ambiguous ending.
The reading she gives is altered, not faithful, so option 0 is contradicted by the text. Her decision happens unstated in the gap between the two paragraphs.
'Scraping it bare, scraping it bare,' placed just before the substitution, works as an image of erasure that anticipates her choice. It does not offer relief from the tension.
'Wholly' and 'every injury' overstate the change, and the image of ice she doesn't trust argues against full forgiveness. The key's account of a guarded daughter beginning to reach toward him fits.
'Ice you don't trust' frames the reconciliation as a fragile thaw. The other options read the cold literally or have no support.

The 'Paid' entries carrying Pruitt's initials show that he knowingly covers the cost himself. Nothing in the text shows Mrs. Danner exploiting him; she plainly states her habit. So 'manipulates' is a misreading, and the keyed reading of quiet mercy is best.

The narration reveals the boy's inner state and his suspicion, so it is not neutral or coolly distant. Because the point of view is limited to the boy, the ledger reveal overturns the reader's judgment as well as his.

She says she forgets to wind the watch, which points away from poverty. The stopped clocks, together with the flag and photograph, suggest time halted by loss, and nothing in the text indicates she cannot afford repairs.

'I had my sentence ready. It sat in my mouth like a coin' shows he still had the words, so choice 3 contradicts the text. He then says 'No, ma'am,' and his own explanation for this is false, which fits the key.

Choice 3 overstates the change ('fully rejected,' 'rest of his life') and is contradicted by the final line, 'I still tell people I would have asked her.' The key's 'unspent coin' reading fits the claim that his faith in payment is unsettled.
'I keep a shop of my own now' identifies the narrator as an adult shopkeeper looking back. This rules out a fifteen-year-old telling the story the same night.
'Though she had not cried' denies that any crying happened, so shame at making her cry is impossible. The line shows him giving himself a false excuse.
The allusion stresses waiting for a husband who may come home, matching her ritual with the watch. Nothing in the text casts Pruitt as a suitor.
'As if it were trying to hear' personifies the house as listening, not as falling down. That supports the reading of a house straining toward news that never comes.
'Paid' with Pruitt's initials overturns the boy's theory that the account is a joke rather than confirming it. Holding it back until the end lets that reversal recast the whole account.
'Stiffness of a thing nobody touches' points to grief that is avoided. The text says nothing about a long military tradition, so choice 0 has no support.

'I still tell people I would have asked her' contradicts 'fully converted' and 'speaks openly.' The key captures the tension: he was shaken in practice but still claims his old hardness when retelling it.
In the simile the doctor 'already knew' the chest 'was sound,' which rules out Pruitt suspecting a hidden flaw. He tends the watch for its owner's sake.

Choices 0 and 1 contradict the text, and choice 3 overgeneralizes ('all old men'). The key matches the passage: the boy reads the ledger as figures, while Pruitt treats the account as a matter of care.

content.text: I upheld the key on all nine questions. Each challenged option is wrong for a reason the text shows, and the line and paragraph references are accurate.

verdicts.reasoning: Option 2 says she believes every kind of pride is a sin. That claim is too broad, and nothing in the text supports it. 'God forgive me' comes just as she grows proud of a success that rests on her deception. Her fall follows at once, which points to guilt about that particular pride.
The text never mentions drilling or coaching. Ann's averted gaze and the class's held breath read as quiet, shared protection. Option 3 adds something the passage doesn't say.

Hetty's question gives away who really teaches the class, and Dask writes a line in his book. 'Nobody laughed' rules out comic relief. Nothing in the text shows resentment or that she knows less than the others.

Option 3 is contradicted by Dask's pointed irony ('under its present master', 'Mr. Penhallow's chest') and by what he says about the coat, which show he understood. Option 1 is a plot summary, not a thesis. Option 2 overgeneralizes.
The lines say the letters were 'answered in a hand that had once been my brother's and was now mine', which matches the keyed answer directly. No other option fits.

The Regulations require a certificated master, and the pupils' strong showing proves she can keep the school. The other options bring in things the text never mentions: a wish to leave, a curate demanding confession, a dislike of teaching.

'It wants wearing' urges her to use the coat, which supports the claim that he gives permission. Option 1 reads the remark as a threat, which undercuts that claim and clashes with the satisfactory report he files. Options 2 and 3 are too literal or rely on outside generalizations about novels.

'They have not yet learned what is wanted' means he values answers that haven't been rehearsed. Option 2's 'trick' and 'betraying' don't fit his grave, kind conduct, or the fact that he protects her once the truth comes out.
She had 'never sat in' the chair. At the end she puts on the coat, sits in the chair and hears the spelling, so she openly takes up the role. She is teaching, not mourning, afraid, or copying Dask.
